q: Talking adult or a wailing kid. Airway next?

opts.t: Airway check is done; move to breathing
opts.why: If they can talk or wail, the path is open.

opts.t: Open with a jaw thrust first
opts.why: A talking path is already open.

opts.t: Suction first even if the mouth is dry
opts.why: Suction only if you see junk or hear gurgling.

opts.t: Put an oral airway in while they talk
opts.why: An oral airway is for fully out, no gag.

q: Unconscious. What is the number-one thing that blocks the path?

opts.t: The tongue
opts.why: Muscles relax. Tongue is the number-one obstruction.

opts.t: Pulmonary edema in the lower airway
opts.why: You only suction what you see or hear up top.

opts.t: A rigid catheter left in place
opts.why: The catheter is a tool, not the first block.

opts.t: A nasal airway that is too short
opts.why: The first block is the floppy tongue.

q: Unconscious airway work. Where do they lie, and where do you stand?

opts.t: They are supine; you are at the top of the head
opts.why: Preferred: supine, you at the crown.

opts.t: They sit up; you stand at the feet
opts.why: Awake people sit themselves. Unconscious work is supine at the head.

opts.t: They are prone; you are at the side
opts.why: Prone is not the airway position.

opts.t: They are on the left side; you are at the feet
opts.why: Recovery is later, and you still work from the head.

q: Found unconscious in bed, no crack on the floor. Which open?

opts.t: Head-tilt chin-lift
opts.why: HTCL only with confidence there is no spinal injury. Bed or a seen couch slump.

opts.t: Jaw thrust
opts.why: Jaw thrust is unknown or possible spine.

opts.t: Leave the tongue down and count breaths first
opts.why: Do not judge breathing until the path is open.

opts.t: Nasal airway before you open the mouth
opts.why: Open first. Adjuncts come after assess and clear.

q: Unconscious on a sidewalk, maybe hit by a car. Which open?

opts.t: Jaw thrust
opts.why: Unknown or possible spine: err caution, jaw thrust.

opts.t: Head-tilt chin-lift
opts.why: HTCL needs a no-spine story.

opts.t: Sit them up and wait
opts.why: Unconscious work is supine at the head.

opts.t: Nasal airway first, then decide
opts.why: Open first. A smashed face would also block a nasal tube.

q: Jaw thrust: where do the hands go, and what happens if you let go?

opts.t: Thumbs on the cheekbones, fingers behind the jaw angle, push up; let go and the tongue drops
opts.why: Jaw up, head still. You are stuck holding it.

opts.t: One hand on the forehead, one under the chin, tilt back; let go and the path stays open
opts.why: That is head-tilt chin-lift, and the tongue still drops if you let go.

opts.t: Fingers in the mouth to scissor it open; let go and the gag starts
opts.why: Cross-finger is a book mouth-open, not the jaw thrust.

opts.t: Hands on the chest, push down; let go and residual volume fills
opts.why: That is not an airway open.

q: What are the four airway steps, in order?

opts.t: Open, assess, clear, maintain
opts.why: Then the airway check, then breathing rate, rhythm, quality.

opts.t: Assess, open, maintain, clear
opts.why: Open is first. Clear is before maintain.

opts.t: Clear, open, assess, maintain
opts.why: Open, then look and listen, then suction if needed.

opts.t: Maintain, assess, open, clear
opts.why: Maintain is last of the four.

q: When is suction indicated?

opts.t: When you see fluid, blood, vomit, or secretions, or you hear gurgling
opts.why: Indication is see it or hear it. Do not invent gurgling.

opts.t: On every unconscious patient, even if the mouth is dry and quiet
opts.why: Nothing seen or heard means do not pick suction.

opts.t: Only after you have bagged for two minutes
opts.why: The two-minute bag is the cycle after a maxed dirty pass.

opts.t: Only if pulse ox is under 94 percent
opts.why: Suction is about junk in the path, not the sat number.

q: Mouth is dirty and suction is not in your hand. First move?

opts.t: Roll them to the side so gravity drains
opts.why: Fastest move is position. Then set up gear.

opts.t: Wait supine until the wall unit is ready
opts.why: Do not wait while junk sits in the path.

opts.t: Bag first so you push the junk down
opts.why: Clear first if you can. Bag-after is only the 10-second / 2-minute cycle.

opts.t: Put a nasal airway in and sit them up
opts.why: Roll now. Adjuncts come after the path is usable.

q: Mouth full of chunks versus down a trach or ET tube. Which catheter?

opts.t: Rigid for the mouth; flexible / non-rigid for a trach or ET tube
opts.why: Rigid has the bigger hole. Flexible clogs on chunks.

opts.t: Flexible for the mouth; rigid for a trach or ET tube
opts.why: Those are swapped.

opts.t: Only the hand-pump, no catheter
opts.why: Hand-pump is the backup unit, not the tip choice.

opts.t: Only the wall unit, no catheter
opts.why: The wall is a power source, not the tip.

q: Start-of-shift vacuum number from the book?

opts.t: More than 300 mmHg
opts.why: Test vacuum. Gage, light, or a glove if there is no gage.

opts.t: More than 40 to 70 mmHg
opts.why: 40-70 psi is an oxygen regulator, not suction.

opts.t: More than 2000 mmHg
opts.why: About 2000 psi is a full oxygen tank.

opts.t: More than 10 mmHg
opts.why: 10 seconds is the suction time cap, not the vacuum.

q: How far does the rigid catheter go?

opts.t: Corner of the mouth to the earlobe, or to the angle of the jaw; only as far as you can see
opts.why: Measure that far. Do not drive it into the trachea.

opts.t: Nose to the earlobe, then into the trachea
opts.why: Nose-to-ear is the nasal-airway measure.

opts.t: Lips to the xiphoid, then sweep a finger
opts.why: That is not the suction measure, and do not fish with a finger.

opts.t: As far as the tube will feed, suction on the way in
opts.why: Insert with suction off, and only as far as you see.

q: When is suction applied?

opts.t: Insert with the hole open; cover the hole and use circles on the way out
opts.why: Insert with suction off. Vacuum on withdrawal.

opts.t: Cover the hole and suction the whole way in
opts.why: No suction on insert.

opts.t: Leave the hole open the whole way out
opts.why: Cover the hole on the way out.

opts.t: Suction only after you bag for two minutes first
opts.why: The two-minute bag is the cycle after a maxed dirty pass.

q: Suction time now, all ages?

opts.t: Until clear, up to 10 seconds
opts.why: One 10-second cap for adult, child, and infant. Then get them oxygen.

opts.t: Adult 15, child 10, infant 5
opts.why: That old split is retired.

opts.t: Until clear, up to 2 minutes
opts.why: Two minutes is the ventilate gap, not the suction cap.

opts.t: Until clear, no time cap
opts.why: There is a 10-second cap.

q: Partner recites adult 15, child 10, infant 5. What is the rule now?

opts.t: They do not do that anymore; one 10-second cap for all ages
opts.why: Old 15/10/5 is retired. Infant may clear in about 2 seconds because there is less volume.

opts.t: Keep 15/10/5 because the book still likes it
opts.why: The lecture retired that split.

opts.t: Use 15 seconds for every age
opts.why: The cap is 10 seconds.

opts.t: Use 5 seconds for every age
opts.why: The cap is 10 seconds, then oxygen.

q: Still dirty at 10 seconds. What cycle?

opts.t: Ventilate 2 minutes, suction up to 10 seconds, repeat
opts.why: No oxygen is 100% dead. That beats a 30-70% aspiration bump.

opts.t: Suction 2 minutes, ventilate 10 seconds, repeat
opts.why: Those times are swapped.

opts.t: Suction 15 seconds, no ventilations
opts.why: 15 is the retired adult number, and they still need air.

opts.t: Stop and put on a nose cannula only
opts.why: They need positive-pressure depth, not a cannula.

q: Blood or vomit that reaches the lungs. What add-on mortality number?

opts.t: Mortality up 30 to 70 percent on top of the original problem
opts.why: Aspiration raises death risk 30-70% on top.

opts.t: Mortality up 10 seconds on top of the original problem
opts.why: 10 seconds is the suction cap.

opts.t: Mortality up 100 percent only if you roll them
opts.why: 100% dead is no oxygen, not the roll.

opts.t: Mortality up 21 percent because room air is 21 percent
opts.why: 21% is room-air oxygen, not this add-on.

q: Catheter keeps clogging on thick chunks. After a retry, what do you stop doing?

opts.t: Stop the same failed pass; roll, drain, scoop with the catheter
opts.why: Log roll and gravity. Scoop with the catheter, not a finger safari.

opts.t: Keep jamming the same clogged pass
opts.why: Stop the failed pass.

opts.t: Sweep with an ungloved finger
opts.why: Do not fish with a finger.

opts.t: Bag hard to blow the chunks into the lungs
opts.why: Roll and drain. Bagging junk down is the least-bad later cycle, not the first clog fix.

q: Pulmonary edema versus what gets suctioned. Which line is right?

opts.t: Edema is lower-airway fluid; you only suction what you see or hear in the upper airway
opts.why: Lower-lung fluid is a different intervention later.

opts.t: Edema is upper-airway junk; suction until the alveoli are dry
opts.why: You cannot suction alveoli.

opts.t: Edema is blood in the chest; decompress it
opts.why: Blood in the chest is hemothorax, and EMT does not decompress.

opts.t: Edema is the tongue; pull it with a finger
opts.why: The tongue is an open-and-hold problem.

q: Who is an oral airway for?

opts.t: Fully unresponsive and no gag
opts.why: OPA = out on AVPU and no gag. Preferred go-to.

opts.t: Semi-conscious with a gag
opts.why: Gag means do not start with OPA.

opts.t: Walking, talking, and asking for it
opts.why: The lecture would not put it in a walking talking person.

opts.t: Any head or face trauma, even with a gag
opts.why: OPA is OK with face trauma only if there is no gag.

q: The oral airway goes in and they gag. What now?

opts.t: Pull it out immediately and get ready for vomit
opts.why: Gag means out now. Expect vomit.

opts.t: Push it farther so the gag stops
opts.why: Farther drives the tongue down and keeps the gag.

opts.t: Tape it and start a nasal airway beside it
opts.why: The oral airway comes out.

opts.t: Leave it and bag through the gag
opts.why: Out immediately.

q: How is an oral airway sized?

opts.t: Corner of the mouth to the earlobe, or to the angle of the jaw
opts.why: Same measure as a rigid suction catheter.

opts.t: Nose to the earlobe, or nose to the jaw angle
opts.why: That is the nasal-airway measure.

opts.t: Lips to the xiphoid
opts.why: That is not the OPA measure.

opts.t: By color code only, no measure
opts.why: Eyeball, then measure. Exact color codes were not given.

q: Which oral-airway insert is acceptable?

opts.t: Upside down and rotate 180, or sideways and rotate 90
opts.why: Both are acceptable. Do not push straight in.

opts.t: Only 180 is allowed; 90 fails the test
opts.why: They will not make 180 versus 90 the only two choices.

opts.t: Push straight in so the tongue goes down
opts.why: Straight in drives the tongue down.

opts.t: Bevel to the septum and feed it up the nose
opts.why: That is nasal-airway placement.

q: Semi-awake, still gags, face uninjured. Which adjunct?

opts.t: Nasal airway
opts.why: NPA is for semi-conscious or unresponsive with a gag, if the face is uninjured.

opts.t: Oral airway
opts.why: A gag is an OPA contraindication.

opts.t: Neither; wait for a stair chair
opts.why: A stair chair is a move tool, not an adjunct.

opts.t: Both at the same time
opts.why: One path. Gag means skip the oral airway.

q: Hard no for a nasal airway?

opts.t: Any head or face trauma
opts.why: Do not wait for blood in the nose. Floor of the nose is the floor of the skull.

opts.t: A gag reflex
opts.why: A gag is a reason to pick NPA, not skip it.

opts.t: They are unresponsive with no gag and no face trauma
opts.why: That patient can take an oral airway first.

opts.t: They are breathing adequately in recovery position
opts.why: Recovery is a maintain option, not an NPA ban.

q: Unresponsive, no gag, obvious facial smash. Which statement is true?

opts.t: Mouth adjunct is allowed; nose adjunct is not
opts.why: OPA is OK with head trauma if no gag. NPA is not.

opts.t: Nose adjunct is allowed; mouth adjunct is not
opts.why: Those are swapped.

opts.t: Both adjuncts are banned
opts.why: OPA is still allowed if there is no gag.

opts.t: Both adjuncts are required
opts.why: One path. NPA is banned with face trauma.

q: They gag on the oral airway and the face is smashed. What is left?

opts.t: Neither tube; hold the jaw until a higher airway arrives
opts.why: Gag kills OPA. Face trauma kills NPA.

opts.t: Force the oral airway past the gag
opts.why: Gag means out.

opts.t: Force the nasal airway past the smash
opts.why: Face trauma bans NPA.

opts.t: Put both tubes in so one can fail
opts.why: Neither tube is safe here.

q: How is a nasal airway sized?

opts.t: Nose to the earlobe, or nose to the angle of the jaw
opts.why: NPA measure is nose to ear or jaw angle.

opts.t: Corner of the mouth to the earlobe, or to the jaw angle
opts.why: That is the oral-airway and suction measure.

opts.t: Lips to the xiphoid
opts.why: That is not the NPA measure.

opts.t: By color code only, no measure
opts.why: Measure nose to ear or jaw.

q: How is a nasal airway placed?

opts.t: Water-based lube, bevel toward the septum, straight in until flush on the nostril
opts.why: Bevel to septum. Right nostril is how they are angled. Single-use, then trash.

opts.t: No lube, bevel away from the septum, stop halfway
opts.why: Water-based lube, bevel to septum, flush on the nostril.

opts.t: Upside down and rotate 180
opts.why: That is an oral-airway insert.

opts.t: Oil-based lube, bevel toward the cheek, then tape it to the forehead
opts.why: Water-based lube and bevel to the middle wall.

q: Unconscious, not injured, still breathing well enough. Which maintain option?

opts.t: Recovery position on the side
opts.why: Recovery is maintain when they breathe well and there is no spine worry. Uncommon, because most need to stay supine to ventilate.

opts.t: Prone, face down
opts.why: Unconscious does not ride prone.

opts.t: Sit them in a stair chair
opts.why: Stair chair is a move tool for awake stairs.

opts.t: Force a nasal airway even with face trauma
opts.why: Face trauma bans NPA.

q: Trapped in a car, not breathing well, fire cutting. Airway versus spine?

opts.t: Urgent move out; someone tries to ventilate in the seat; spine may wait
opts.why: A and B are life. Spine is quality of life. May sacrifice spine protection to keep them alive.

opts.t: Finish a full board in the seat before any air
opts.why: They need air now.

opts.t: Wait for a stair chair
opts.why: A stair chair is not the wreck tool.

opts.t: Leave them and set up a wall suction unit first
opts.why: Ventilate in the seat if you can, then get them out.

q: Three suction units, and which one goes on scene?

opts.t: Hand-pump is backup; battery portable goes on scene; wall is in the ambulance
opts.why: Check charge at the start of shift. Dead battery means the hand pump.

opts.t: Wall unit goes on scene; hand-pump stays in the hospital; battery is backup only
opts.why: Battery portable is the scene unit.

opts.t: Only the wall unit exists
opts.why: Three were named: hand-pump, battery, wall.

opts.t: Only a finger sweep is used on scene
opts.why: The scene unit is battery portable.

q: What is the sterile water jug for during suction?

opts.t: Flush the line between passes so blood and vomit do not clot it
opts.why: Suction water between passes.

opts.t: Give them a drink after suction
opts.why: The jug is for the tubing, not a drink.

opts.t: Fill the oxygen humidifier on a D tank lying on its side
opts.why: That jug-on-a-D-tank idea is a later oxygen talk, and it spills.

opts.t: Wash the tongue before a jaw thrust
opts.why: The jug clears the suction line.

q: After suction, what is trash versus what is sprayed?

opts.t: Catheter and tubing are trash; canister goes to biohazard; the machine is spray-disinfected
opts.why: Sterile wrap, single-patient path. Keep a packaged set with the unit.

opts.t: The machine is trash; the catheter is washed and reused on the next patient
opts.why: Catheter and tubing are single-patient trash.

opts.t: Everything is saved for the next call
opts.why: The fluid path is single-patient.

opts.t: Only the wall unit is thrown away
opts.why: The machine stays. The path is trash.

q: After suction they still cannot clear themselves. What depth of air?

opts.t: Positive pressure depth, not a nose cannula or simple mask
opts.why: They probably are not breathing adequately. They need a bag, not a cannula.

opts.t: A nose cannula at 1 liter
opts.why: A cannula is not enough depth here.

opts.t: A simple mask at 2 liters
opts.why: They need positive pressure.

opts.t: No air until the next 15-second suction
opts.why: The cap is 10 seconds, then they get oxygen.
